data.title: StarHub merges with M1 for S$1.1 billion; acquires Circles Life Singapore
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] StarHub announced on Tuesday (Nov 24) that it will be merging with Keppel’s M1 for S$1.1 billion.

The deal, subject to regulatory approval given by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), is expected to be closed by the first half of 2027.

Earlier in September, both StarHub and Keppel confirmed that they were in talks over a potential deal regarding an acquisition of M1 with no certainty of a deal happening, following reports by The Business Times.

StarHub also announced on Tuesday that it has exercised its call option to acquire the Singapore operations of mobile virtual network operator Circles Life.

StarHub and M1 were reported to have explored a potential merger back in 2024, but no deal materialised.

The potential StarHub and M1 deal comes following a collapsed S$1.4 billion deal between Simba and M1 in May, after the IMDA suspended its assessment of the transaction while investigating Simba’s unauthorised spectrum usage.

Simba subsequently admitted to the unauthorised usage on Nov 17 with the IMDA reviewing the telco’s response to the regulator’s show cause notice, and is assessing if Simba’s response covers all areas that the IMDA is investigating.

Following the proposed acquisition, the number of mobile network operators in Singapore would reduce from four to three.

According to data from Bloomberg Intelligence, Singtel leads with roughly 43 per cent of the mobile subscriber share, followed by M1 at around 22 per cent, StarHub at 21 per cent and then Simba at 14 per cent, as at June.

The S$1.1 billion deal is below Simba’s original bid and is in-line with analysts estimates earlier in September.

Foo Zhiwei, analyst at Macquarie Capital, estimated the enterprise value of M1 to be at between S$1.16 billion and S$1.25 billion while Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Chris Muckensturm puts it at between S$1.1 billion and S$1.2 billion.

Analysts attributed the lower valuation to weaker domestic consumer revenue caused by competition, as well as the migration of MyRepublic’s 4G wholesale business from M1 to StarHub.

Shares of StarHub closed S$0.01 or 1 per cent lower at S$1.01 on Monday, while shares of Keppel closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent lower at S$8.83, before the announcement was made.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Singapore raises 2026 growth forecast to ‘around 6%’; Q3 GDP revised up at 6.1%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Republic has upgraded its full-year growth forecast for 2026 to “around 6 per cent”, from the 4.5 to 5.5 per cent range set in August, as strong global artificial intelligence-related demand continues to drive its trade-reliant economy.

This was as third-quarter gross domestic product grew 6.1 per cent year on year, easing from the 6.4 per cent growth recorded in the second quarter, according to data from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) on Tuesday (Nov 24).

The Q3 figure was revised up from the advance estimate of 5.4 per cent, which was largely based on data for July and August. For the first three quarters of 2026, the economy grew 6.2 per cent.

On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, GDP expanded 1.5 per cent, moderating from the 1.8 per cent growth in Q2.

The wholesale trade, manufacturing, and finance and insurance sectors drove Q3 growth, METI said.

Growth in the machinery, equipment and supplies segment of wholesale trade, as well as the electronics and precision engineering clusters of manufacturing, was boosted by strong AI-related demand.

Meanwhile, the expansion in the finance and insurance sector was underpinned by credit growth and fee-generating activities, said the ministry.

In contrast, the retail trade and F&B services sectors contracted, partly due to a sustained shift in local spending abroad as outbound travel increased, it added.

Growth to ease in 2027

METI said AI-related production and exports, driven by a stronger-than-expected build-out of data centres, have continued to accelerate since August, and that momentum is expected to last through the rest of the year.

While elevated energy prices have fuelled global inflationary pressures and tighter monetary policy in several economies, the ministry assessed that, on balance, Singapore’s external demand outlook has improved compared with August.

Strong AI-related demand will continue to drive the manufacturing and wholesale trade sectors, while outward-oriented services such as finance and insurance, and information and communications should remain resilient.

The accommodation sector will be supported by strong hotel bookings amid a robust line-up of events. The outlook for retail trade and F&B, however, remains subdued.

For 2027, METI projected full-year growth of 2.5 to 4.5 per cent, as the pace of new AI investments is expected to ease from its high level this year.

Growth in most of Singapore’s key trading partners is also projected to soften, it added.

The ministry expects oil supply from the Middle East to recover gradually, which should ease global energy prices and inflationary pressures over the course of the year.

The US economy is expected to slow as restrictive monetary policy and weaker real wage growth weigh on investment and consumption. China is also set to slow as export growth softens and consumption stays sluggish.

The eurozone, by contrast, is forecast to pick up, helped by firmer household spending and defence-related manufacturing, said METI.

Growth in key South-east Asian economies is projected to ease as AI investments and AI-related exports moderate.

Domestically, the electronics and precision engineering clusters and the machinery, equipment and supplies segment of wholesale trade will continue to be supported by AI demand, although at a slower pace.

Transport engineering should benefit from multi-year capacity expansions in the aerospace segment and strong aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul orders, while the information and communications sector will get a lift from demand for digital transformation and AI-related services.

Consumer-facing sectors such as retail trade and F&B services may continue to be weighed down by the shift in local spending abroad.

Sector growth

Three downside risks remain, said METI. Concerns over the sustainability of the global AI cycle could trigger sharper corrections in financial markets, with potential spillovers to the broader economy.

Further escalation of the Middle East conflict could cause fresh spikes in energy and other input prices, stoking inflation and tightening global financial conditions. Economic and political uncertainties in external economies could also weigh on investment and consumption.

The ministry said it will monitor developments closely and adjust the forecast over the course of 2026 if necessary.

The goods-producing industries expanded 8.3 per cent year on year in Q3, slowing from 11.2 per cent in the previous quarter.

Manufacturing output grew 8.5 per cent on the year, moderating from the 13.2 per cent growth in the previous quarter. Output expansions in the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters outweighed declines in the chemicals and biomedical manufacturing clusters.

Sequentially, however, the sector contracted 0.2 per cent, a reversal from the 6.5 per cent expansion in Q2.

The construction sector grew 9.5 per cent year on year, faster than the 6.5 per cent growth in the previous quarter, supported by both public and private-sector works.

Quarter on quarter, construction output grew 3.6 per cent, a turnaround from the 2.4 per cent contraction in Q2.

The services-producing industries, meanwhile, grew at a quicker pace of 6.1 per cent year on year, up from 5.4 per cent in Q2. On a quarterly basis, they expanded 1.9 per cent, compared with 1.1 per cent previously.

Wholesale trade expanded 14.5 per cent year on year, accelerating from 9.8 per cent in Q2.

Wholesale volumes of telecommunications and computers, and electronic components rose on strong global demand for AI-related electronics, while volumes in the fuels and chemicals segment fell, affected by oil supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict.

Sequentially, the sector grew 6.5 per cent, versus 0.5 per cent in Q2.

The information and communications sector grew 6.2 per cent year on year, picking up from 4.7 per cent in Q2, driven by data centre operations and Internet search engine activities.

Finance and insurance expanded 3.8 per cent year on year, slowing from 6.2 per cent in the previous quarter. Banks, fund managers and securities dealers saw a more modest increase in fee and commission incomes amid more selective risk-taking by investors, although credit intermediation remained strong.

Quarter on quarter, the sector contracted 3 per cent, a reversal from the 0.9 per cent growth in Q2.

The real estate sector grew 4.7 per cent year on year, compared with 5 per cent in Q2, while administrative and support services expanded 3.6 per cent, faster than the 2.7 per cent growth previously.

Growth in the accommodation sector slowed to 0.9 per cent year on year from 1.9 per cent, and transportation and storage grew 2.2 per cent, easing from 3.6 per cent.

Retail trade shrank 2.7 per cent on the year, reversing a 0.8 per cent expansion in Q2, with both motor vehicular and non-motor vehicular sales volumes falling.

F&B services contracted 2.1 per cent, worsening from a 1.3 per cent decline.

data.title: Singapore ups full-year exports forecast to 30-32% for 2026
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore is now headed for export growth of 30 to 32 per cent in 2026, with trade agency Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) citing “exceptionally strong performance” and “continued support from artificial intelligence-related demand” as it upped the non-oil domestic exports (NODX) forecast.

The fresh upgrade to the full-year NODX outlook comes as NODX grew by 45.8 per cent year on year in the three months to September, according to a quarterly review released by EnterpriseSG on Tuesday (Nov 24) morning.

The double-digit export growth notched in the third quarter extended gains from the expansion of 27.4 per cent in the second quarter, which had prompted EnterpriseSG to bump its official forecast range to 14 to 16 per cent – up from 3 to 5 per cent previously.

But NODX growth is expected to moderate to 5 to 7 per cent in 2027 from this year’s high base, with EnterpriseSG also warning that downside risks include “a sharper-than-expected correction in AI-related demand and prolonged conflict in the Middle East”.

Tariffs ‘took a backseat’

While the US government’s tariff-heavy approach to international trade was a concern earlier in 2026, significant carve-outs for semiconductors and pharmaceuticals – key industries for Singapore’s manufacturing sector – have eased some of the initial worry.

“Tariff concerns have clearly taken a backseat,” Selena Ling, chief economist at OCBC, told The Business Times, citing “exceptional electronics NODX performance” in 2026.

Third-quarter NODX continued to be fuelled by electronics exports, which surged by a record 117 cent year on year – up from growth of 88.1 in the second quarter.

The electronics cluster saw year-on-year increases in shipments of integrated circuits (83.2 per cent), disk media products (313.7 per cent) and personal computers (166.3 per cent).

NODX growth was also supported by the non-electronics sector, with shipments rising by 20.8 per cent in the third quarter, against 8 per cent previously.

EnterpriseSG attributed the increase to “support from the lumpy exports of structures of ships and boats”, as well as to growth in shipments of specialised machinery (40.2 per cent) and non-monetary gold (70.1 per cent).

Ling cautioned that Singapore exports’ strong performance in 2026 “could also have been due to frontloading ahead of anticipated tariffs”, while uplift from AI capex globally will also make normalisation likely on the back of a “more challenging” base effect in 2027.

Moody’s Analytics senior economist Denise Cheok noted that AI-related demand “has provided a buffer against tariffs and geopolitical headwinds”.

But, pointing to growing investor jitters over AI financing and valuations, as well as uncertainty over regulations on AI use and data centre operations, she told BT: “The growing reliance on the AI boom leaves the economy increasingly vulnerable to a correction.”

‘AI bubble’? Probably not

Asked whether the electronics sector could take a hit from curbs imposed by the US on high-tech AI chip exports to South-east Asia, Maybank economist Brian Lee told BT that the new restrictions should have a limited direct impact on Singapore exports – though “there could be second-order impact on electronic demand if data centre investment in the region slows”.

Vishrut Rana, senior economist at S&P Global Ratings, noted that developments such as fresh US chip export controls and market concerns about high AI-related infrastructure spending “could dampen global investment plans in coming quarters”.

But “there is a strong order pipeline for electronics infrastructure from Asian economies”, he told BT. Though industry hyperscalers – the cloud and data centre operators enabling AI expansion – have guided for a slowdown in capex growth, S&P Global Ratings still estimates that capex from the top hyperscaler players will be even larger in 2027 than in 2026.

If the hyperscalers were to pull back on investments simultaneously, they would risk triggering a sudden collapse in the global AI industry, which “could hit semiconductors, advanced packaging, equipment and Singapore’s associated trade and manufacturing activity”, said Ling – but added that such an “AI bubble scenario” is not her base case.

Said Cheok from Moody’s: “A financial correction might not necessarily cause tech exports to collapse. The bursting of the dotcom bubble in the early 2000s did not end the build-out of communications infrastructure. Likewise, an AI bust is unlikely to end demand for chips.”

Trading partners

In the third quarter of 2026, Singapore saw overall growth in NODX to the Republic’s top markets, led by the US (74.4 per cent), mainland China (46.6 per cent) and Taiwan (58.5 per cent).

Electronics NODX growth was driven by the US, Taiwan and South Korea, while non-electronics NODX growth was driven by mainland China, Hong Kong and South Korea.

Total merchandise trade expanded by 44.4 per cent, compared with 40 per cent in the second quarter, while total services trade rose by 14.6 per cent, after rising by 12.1 per cent previously.

data.title: Why Jensen Huang and Nvidia matter so much to markets
data.description:
THE decision by Nvidia’s board of directors to restore Jensen Huang as chief executive officer on Nov 23 after President Donald Trump pressed for the move speaks to the enormous impact both of Huang on the company and of the company on the larger stock market.

The sharp decline in Nvidia’s stock price that began after news emerged that Huang had had an affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Chinese intelligence erased more than two trillion dollars of value from the stock market, which Trump has long cited as a metric for his presidency.

It was Huang’s decision to pivot Nvidia’s focus from graphics chips for gaming to the artificial intelligence “accelerators” that made it one the world’s biggest companies by market value.

At its peak, in early October, Nvidia’s market capitalisation totalled around US$5.8 trillion, a figure larger than the national economic output of Germany.

Huang’s globe-trotting lobbying helped to maintain its dominant position. Hence the sharp sell-off of Nvidia’s shares that began when the espionage scandal first raised questions about his future at the company and continued after he resigned on Nov 12.

The trend began to reverse after the leather-jacketed, celebrity co-founder’s reinstatement as CEO. 

Here’s why the stakes in this saga have been so high.

Market titan

On Nov 30, 2022, a then-little-known company called OpenAI released a chatbot called ChatGPT, triggering an explosion in demand for a type of computing chip that Nvidia was uniquely well-placed to provide. Over the next few years, Nvidia’s share price rose 14-fold before peaking in early October.

The company witnessed soaring demand from data-centre customers, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft. In mid-2024, it overtook all three by market capitalization for the first time. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company to surpass both US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market value. 

By early October, it was closing in on the US$6 trillion mark. However, investors were becoming increasingly skittish over frothy AI stock valuations and an industry borrowing spree, and Nvidia fell behind Apple as the world’s biggest company. 

Following the revelations about Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese agent, reports of an affair with another woman who worked for him, and his resignation, Nvidia’s valuation fell to about US$3 trillion as of Nov 20, the Friday before Huang was reinstated. The news that he’d returned to the company sent the valuation shooting back upward.

Chip supremacy

Nvidia accounts for an overwhelming share of sales of the advanced chips that process AI tasks. Its dominance partly reflects a substantial head start: Years before AI really took off, the company was investing in ways to sell its graphics processing units for uses beyond gaming.

It maintained that lead by rolling out new designs every year. Its size and purchasing power kept it ahead of the game, making it harder for smaller rivals to keep up. 

The leadership turmoil came at an especially bad time. Nvidia’s rivals, and even some of its customers, are working hard to develop competitive AI chips.

A raft of startups are raising billions of dollars from investors keen to back the next breakthrough.

Competition is also intensifying in China, where the company is prevented by US export controls from selling its most advanced products. Companies such as Huawei Technologies — blacklisted in the US — are making rapid strides in developing homegrown AI chips, Nvidia has said. 

AI finance linchpin

Since 2024, Nvidia has become not just a supplier to the AI industry but also one of its key financial backers. It has invested heavily in leading AI platform developers including OpenAI, Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Mistral of France, as well as companies building AI data centres. It’s a symbiotic relationship: Nvidia helps to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure, stoking demand for Nvidia’s chips. 

Portfolio dominance

Until mid-2020, Nvidia’s market capitalisation represented less than 1 per cent of the total value of all the companies tracked in the S&P 500 index, the standard benchmark for the US stock market.

For much of the past two years, Nvidia’s share hovered around 8 per cent, the largest slice of any company. In the wake of Huang’s troubles, Nvidia’s share of the total value fell to 5 per cent as of Nov 20.

Because of the company’s weight, its health can significantly affect the overall value of the S&P 500, to which enormous amounts of money are tied. Some US$20 trillion in assets is either indexed or benchmarked to it, according to S&P Global. These are held largely through retirement funds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

Key-man risk

Huang has been known for his exacting management style at Nvidia, even in an industry full of domineering CEOs who obsess over details.

In his previous role as CEO, every major decision flowed through him, and he weighed in on even the most minute aspects of the business. Huang had about 60 people reporting to him directly, far more than the average tech leader. They sent him emails with “top five things” that he read and responded to at all hours.

The scandals involving Huang underscored Nvidia’s “key-man” risk: The 63-year-old executive was seen as inseparable from the company’s success. Huang’s exit had put Nvidia in an unusually vulnerable position for a company of its size: There was no one designated to replace him. BLOOMBERG

data.title: The trillion-dollar question behind the AI trade
data.description:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence is real. I know because it has changed how my own team works.

Venture capital used to start with a lot of digging. We trawled databases and news flow for companies worth a call. A first read of a sector used to eat most of an associate’s week.

Now, AI agents do the first pass. It takes an afternoon, and the time saved goes into calling customers and checking what the founder told us. Our investment committee papers are drafted by AI and edited by people. It used to be the other way round.

We even built our own software. Using AI coding tools, our team put together a venture operating system that tracks every deal from first lead to portfolio, and prepares our limited partner (LP) reports.

Nobody on the team is a software engineer. A year ago, this would have meant a six-figure contract with a vendor. This year, it was a side project.

However, being useful and making money are different things. That gap is what the AI trade now hinges on.

A record listing in a nervous market

On Nov 19, Anthropic, the maker of Claude, listed on Nasdaq in the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record, raising about US$81.3 billion. Its shares closed the first day 17 per cent above the IPO price, valuing the company at roughly US$1.76 trillion.

That vote of confidence came in a nervous market. The Nasdaq 100 had fallen about 13 per cent from its early-October peak. Two days before the listing, Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of US$115.8 billion, more than double that of the year before, yet its shares kept sliding.

Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive the week before. Washington also tightened export controls, requiring licences for advanced chips shipped to several countries, including Singapore and Malaysia.

There is also a deeper worry about money. More and more of the build-out is financed through what look like circular deals between chipmakers and the AI labs that buy from them.

Alongside the IPO, Anthropic raised another US$26 billion through a private placement with strategic partners including Google and Nvidia. That is not irrational, but it makes it harder to tell how much demand comes from real customers and how much is money circling within the industry.

The listing tells us investors will pay a premium for an AI lab with fast-growing revenue. It does not tell us whether the infrastructure behind it will earn a return.

How big is the hurdle?

Moody’s expects hyperscaler capital spending to reach about US$785 billion this year and approach US$1 trillion in 2027. Goldman Sachs is more bullish, expecting the five largest to spend about US$1.2 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027.

Call it US$1 trillion a year, and assume for simplicity that three-quarters goes to AI, since about a quarter will probably go to replacing ageing servers and storage in the traditional cloud business. That is US$750 billion a year.

Now some rough maths. Microsoft and Google depreciate their servers over six years in their own accounts, so I will use the same life. Each year of spending adds about US$125 billion of depreciation. Keep spending US$750 billion a year from 2027, and by the early 2030s, you would end up with about US$4.5 trillion of AI infrastructure, depreciating at US$750 billion a year.

Depreciation is only part of the bill. At AWS, other operating costs, from power to staff and sales, run at roughly twice depreciation. Apply the same ratio, and US$750 billion of depreciation comes with about US$1.5 trillion of other costs, for total operating costs of about US$2.25 trillion a year.

Now assume a 25 per cent operating margin, below the roughly 30 per cent AWS earned before the boom in large language models. Covering those costs at that margin takes US$3 trillion of AI revenue a year.

And that is only what the cloud providers must earn. Apps like Anthropic’s Claude pay them for compute and keep their own margin on top. Assume a 50 per cent gross margin for the apps, roughly midway between Anthropic’s and its Chinese rivals’. Then end-users would have to spend about US$6 trillion a year.

So where are we today? Anthropic’s annualised revenue reached about US$81 billion at the end of October, according to its prospectus. OpenAI’s is about US$50 billion on Bloomberg’s count. Add the big cloud providers’ own AI businesses, and Western AI revenue comes to roughly US$200 billion a year.

Getting from there to US$6 trillion means growing around 30-fold within seven years, or about 63 per cent growth a year. On this year’s form, that growth looks almost easy: Anthropic’s run rate has grown about nine-fold since January. However, no industry has kept up that pace from this base for years on end.

To be fair to the labs, the economics at the top can work. Anthropic’s prospectus showed an operating profit of US$974 million on US$11.6 billion of revenue in the second quarter, its first quarterly operating profit.

Its gross margin is about 85 per cent, which means it keeps about 85 cents of every revenue dollar after the cost of serving customers.

The question is whether the whole system can earn its keep at the level of capex already committed.

Can productivity gains alone justify the investment?

AI can automate a lot of tasks, but I do not believe it can completely replace jobs. Judgment and accountability still matter, and these stay with people. Someone still has to sign the investment memo and face the LPs when a deal goes wrong.

What AI does is make people faster, and stretch what one person can do. A venture investor can run more deals at once, and can now be a novice UI designer and a novice engineer at the same time.

Which brings me to my favourite test. If Vertex cut off my Claude access tomorrow, would I pay for it myself? Almost certainly, because it buys me back precious hours with my family. To me, that is the truest measure of whether an AI tool is worth anything.

Companies sign off software budgets without much thought. People are far stingier with their own money.

But apply that test to everyone, and the price gets steep. International Labour Organization data puts the world’s knowledge workers at roughly 800 million. Assume every one of them uses AI and spread US$6 trillion among them; each would need to pay about US$7,500 a year, or roughly US$625 a month.

That is a far cry from what companies pay today. A standard business seat for Claude or ChatGPT lists at US$20 to US$25 a month, and even the premium seats for heavy users cost about US$100.

For a professional on US$60,000 in Singapore or New York, US$625 a month is about 12.5 per cent of pay. That is a real bite, even for an enthusiast like me. For a worker on US$25,000, it is 30 per cent. And if only half of knowledge workers sign up, the bill per head doubles.

What about agents taking over work outright? They may not replace whole jobs, but they can take over chunks of them, from customer service to routine coding.

Bank of America puts global wages in seven white-collar functions, from sales to IT, at about US$18.6 trillion a year, and expects agents to handle a 10th of that work by 2030. Yet even this will not cover the capex.

Employers will switch to AI only if the savings are meaningful, so the AI bill has to come in well below the wages it replaces. Bank of America assumes the companies selling these agents capture only about 8 per cent of the roughly US$1.9 trillion that this work is worth, or about US$155 billion a year by 2030. Spending on AI will be a fraction of the wage bill it displaces.

So neither selling seats nor taking over tasks is likely to close the gap on its own. For that, AI has to do things that simply are not possible today.

From productivity to breakthroughs

AI can create value in two ways. The first is doing existing work faster or cheaper. Make a lawyer a fifth faster, and most of the gain goes to the law firm or its clients.

The second – and far bigger – prize is doing work that was not possible before. There are early signs that this is arriving. In May, an OpenAI model disproved a conjecture in geometry first posed by Paul Erdos in 1946, overturning what mathematicians had believed for nearly 80 years.

It was the first time AI had autonomously solved a prominent open problem in mathematics, and it came from a general-purpose model, not one built for the task.

A far bigger claim came last week. Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, released a proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he says he found working with Claude. Posed in 1859, it is arguably the most famous open problem in mathematics, with a US$1 million prize attached.

The proof was written in Lean, a language that lets computers check every step, and the Lean community certified it the next day. Mathematicians are still digesting what it means.

Science is moving the same way. The scientists behind AlphaFold, which predicts how proteins fold, shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and models are now designing new proteins from scratch. A new drug typically takes a decade and billions of dollars to develop, cutting years off that is worth far more than a faster scientist.

Problems like these are hard and long unsolved, and some could be worth trillions of dollars. Think of developing better cancer treatments. When the prize is that big, the willingness to spend on tokens, the units AI companies charge by, will be far higher than for any productivity tool. A drugmaker chasing a cure will gladly pay for as much compute as it takes.

Beyond the lab, robots that can see and reason could take on work that has resisted automation for decades, and AI doctors and tutors could reach millions in our region who have never had good access to either.

If I were a public investor, I would be looking for more data points that these breakthroughs are coming, and that customers are paying enough for them to start closing the spending gap behind the capex.

For those of us in South-east Asia and India, there are two lessons. First, the region is hosting a big slice of the build-out, from data centres in Johor to chip assembly in Penang.

Hosting the capex is not the same as owning the returns, and we should be honest about which side of the ledger we sit on. If the hyperscalers overbuild and then pause, it is the data centres in Johor and the plants in Penang that will feel the hangover.

Second, be wary of startups that simply resell productivity seats. If even the giants struggle to charge US$625 a month, a local wrapper will struggle more.

Our best opportunity lies in companies that use AI to do what could not be done before in our own markets, such as diagnosing patients where doctors are scarce, and that charge for the result. If the infrastructure has been overbuilt, falling compute prices will be a gift to them.

The railway booms of the 19th century ruined many of the investors who financed them, yet they built the modern economy. AI can be real and still disappoint the people paying for it. The trade will be vindicated only if what customers get turns into revenue big enough to pay for the infrastructure.

The writer is executive director of investment at Vertex Ventures South-east Asia and India. The views expressed are his own.

data.title: US stocks bounce back; Nvidia shares shoot up 31% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO
data.description:
US STOCKS surged on Monday (Nov 23), led by a big jump in the Nasdaq as Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares after last week’s rout.

Nvidia’s shares shot up as much as 36.6 per cent after the board returned Huang. He had resigned from the company on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

US President Donald Trump said he secured a deal with Nvidia’s board to bring back Huang as CEO. Nvidia is widely seen as a cornerstone of the AI trade.

The news helped Wall Street recover from last week’s sharp selloff. On Friday, the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections as worries mounted about the AI trade.

The Nasdaq-100 added more than US$2 trillion in market value on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 had their biggest daily gains since the market surged after Trump paused his “Liberation Day” tariff package in April 2025.

“The thought had been, and it’s being borne out today, that Jensen Huang is uniquely important to Nvidia and to the AI trade,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments.

Still, he said, “you have one issue that is resolved - and it’s a biggie - but you still have to see how the rest of things play out.”

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01 per cent, to 49,595.31, the S&P 500 rose 326.78 points, or 4.73 per cent, to 7,237.17 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1,471.83 points, or 6.51 per cent, to 24,089.56.

Before Monday, the Nasdaq had come close to entering a bear market as investors worried about the heavy borrowing underpinning AI investment and questioned whether the sector could deliver sufficient returns.

Fears of political scrutiny also mounted after Democrats swept the US midterm elections.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and S&P 500 information technology sector both were sharply higher on Monday, along with megacap stocks such as Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet.

Also climbing were neocloud and data-center companies, which had come under sharp selling pressure following Huang’s abrupt exit. Other sectors also rose, with energy being the only group in negative territory.

“We don’t think the rebound has run its course, and at these levels, it’s not too late to gradually add back technology exposure,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Ahead this week is Wednesday’s personal consumption expenditures report, which could give clues about the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook. REUTERS

data.title: The problem when your software supplier starts doing your job, too
data.description:
IF YOU have ever bought software for a business, this arrangement might seem familiar. The supplier provides the software. You run the business and hire the employees who use it. Everyone understands their role.

But that arrangement is starting to change. Artificial intelligence agents can now use tools and complete tasks across different applications, taking on work that previously needed someone on your team.

The appeal is there. You wanted customers served and accounts reconciled. The software was supposed to help with that, and the employees were supposed to operate it. But if agents can operate the software, why do you still need the employees?

For years, you bought a licence and installed the software yourself. Then came software as a service, with a subscription and hosting handled by the supplier. The employees still did the work.

With agents, the supplier can now sell you the finished work itself. You pay for the outcome, and running the software becomes the supplier’s concern.

Suppliers are taking on different amounts of that work. Qualified’s Piper agent talks to potential customers, qualifies leads and books meetings. Your company still runs the sales operation, but staff no longer have to handle every initial enquiry themselves. Crescendo goes further, offering to manage customer service for you using AI agents and human specialists.

Superunit takes it a step further. You just need to pay for a completed employment check. Its agents track down the employer, make the calls and follow up.

If they can confirm the details, you get the result and a record of how they checked it. If they cannot, there is no charge. You do not need someone on your payroll to make those calls, chase a reply or supervise the agents. Even the music that is played when a customer is placed on hold becomes the supplier’s problem.

The end of traditional outsourced work?

Businesses have outsourced work for years, of course. A supplier might organise it more efficiently, but taking on another account generally meant hiring more people. Agents let the supplier take on more customers without hiring at the same rate. If they do enough of the work reliably, the supplier can quote a price that your own team or a traditional outsourcer would struggle to match.

We often hear that “AI won’t replace you, but someone using AI will”. This passes for career advice, though it also works quite well as a threat.

Employees are encouraged to become that someone by learning to supervise agents. Unfortunately, managing the agents may already be included in the supplier’s fee. There may indeed be a new role overseeing AI agents, but someone at the supplier may already have it.

Your company may still need people to approve the results. In Qurrent’s case study about Roofstock, agents prepare accounting documents and perform checks, while property accountants control what goes into the books.

Those accountants approve the work, rather than manage the agents. But checking it may take fewer people than preparing it. You could serve more customers with the same team, or the same number with fewer people. Moving everyone into “higher-value work” is an aspiration, not a staffing plan.

For those who stay, the working day could become harder. Once agents handle the routine requests, employees may spend more of their time on disputes, unusual cases and customers who have already lost patience. The routine work disappears, along with the breathing space between difficult cases.

Junior employees could also lose the chance to learn on the job. A junior accountant learns by tracking down why two figures do not match, with a colleague checking their reasoning. Next time, they know where to look. Give them a finished reconciliation to approve, and they have the responsibility without the experience.

If those opportunities disappear, where will the next generation of experienced staff come from? Hiring from another company just passes the problem along.

If you run a service business, the risk extends beyond your employees. The work you hand to an AI company may be the very service your customers pay you for.

Suppose you own a call centre. A retailer pays you to handle its customer calls, and you pay an AI company to answer routine enquiries such as “Where’s my order?” When your contract comes up for renewal, the AI company could bid for the whole account.

It already handles the routine calls. If it can put its own people on the difficult ones, the retailer can hire it directly. You could lose the contract to the very company you hired to help deliver it.

Even if you keep part of the account, the retailer could give the AI company all the routine calls and send you only the complaints. Your team would still have to calm the customer whose parcel has gone missing for the second time. You could end up with a smaller contract and a harder working day.

This move from providing technology to delivering the service is already happening in professional services. Eudia offers legal services through Eudia Counsel, combining its technology with lawyers.

Norm AI has set up an affiliated law firm, Norm Law, where agents do the initial work and lawyers review it. A general counsel can now send them a contract to review. That puts them in contention for work that might otherwise have gone to an established law firm.

Consulting firms face a similar situation with their AI partners. Ode with Anthropic helps companies work out where to use AI and builds the systems for them. OpenAI’s Deployment Company sends engineers into businesses to redesign processes and put AI into use. Their consulting partners sell these services, too.

You began by asking whether you still needed employees to operate the software. If you run a service business, your customers could make much the same calculation about your company. The AI company you hired to cut your costs would be well placed to offer them a quote.

Buying the work may have looked like a straightforward way to save money. But if your supplier can deliver the service, too, the question is whether customers will still need you at all.

The writer works in Singapore’s public service and has been in the tech industry for more than 30 years

data.title: Huang’s return to Nvidia followed unprecedented intervention by Trump
data.description:
PRESIDENT Donald Trump and his AI-friendly allies believed only Jensen Huang could revive Nvidia’s fortunes and reverse a massive stock-market slide. So they went to work to reinstate the beleaguered tech titan.

In what amounted to an unprecedented intervention into the fate of a publicly traded company, Trump acknowledged speaking directly to Nvidia’s board over the weekend to bring Huang back. It paid off: On Monday, Nvidia announced Huang would return as chief executive officer. Nvidia’s stock soared 36 per cent, lifting the broader market with it.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump told CNBC on Monday morning after Nvidia announced its decision. “I said, ‘Boy that’s a rocket ship going in the wrong direction.’ Now it’s going in the right direction.” 

A person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private deliberations, said Trump and Vice-President JD Vance had been briefed on the national-security elements of the situation and didn’t see any evidence that Huang had done anything illegal or jeopardised national security. 

The person said Trump believes that working closely with Huang gives the government the best opportunity to protect national security. With that in mind, Trump and Vance worked with the board and helped it decide to reinstate him, according to the person.

The surprise decision to reinstate Huang — despite admissions of at least two affairs, including with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence — was the result of a sustained pressure campaign not only from Trump but from numerous allies who argued the CEO was too important to the fate of the company and the US economy writ large.

Trump had been frank about his desire to see the Nvidia chief return to the top of the company fuelling the artificial intelligence sector with its advanced chips.

The episode underscored just how far he was willing to go, and how central the stock market is to Trump’s decision-making.

The Nvidia chief has been the highest-profile cheerleader for the artificial intelligence industry, and his company has sought to propel adoption of the technology with billions of dollars in investment in other AI businesses.

His departure after an affair with an alleged Chinese spy risked derailing the sector’s future growth, just as Democratic gains in the Nov 3 midterm elections threatened the US data centre construction boom.

While Trump declared victory on Monday, the move also poses a risk for the White House, especially if investigations now underway by the Justice Department and Nvidia’s board uncover more questionable behaviour, reveal that Huang’s actions put US national security at risk or show that he was compromised by Chinese intelligence.

“Nvidia is taking a huge risk considering they don’t know what kind or magnitude of evidence the CIA has of espionage,” said Dennis Wilder, an ex-CIA and White House official who is now at Georgetown University.

It’s still unclear if more will come to light.

Jensen Huang has already acknowledged affairs with a subordinate and with Alice Huang, a Chinese woman who had been a top executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre operator that helped flood South-east Asia with billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia chips. 

US authorities are now investigating whether some of the chips Megaspeed bought may have been diverted to China in violation of export controls, potentially giving Chinese firms — and reportedly the Chinese military — a computing boost as they seek to compete with American AI developers.

Multiple reports have alleged Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, which operates both domestically and abroad. 

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Alice Huang is no longer employed there. She is now in China, Bloomberg News has reported. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously rejected the spying claims as “unsubstantiated.” 

US lawmakers — including Republicans as well as Democrats who will take over the House and Senate in January — are demanding to know what information underpinned Trump’s assurances to Nvidia.

Huang’s reinstatement alarmed Republican China hawks, including former US House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

“There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as CEO of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” Gingrich wrote on social media.

For the time being, Huang’s allies are heralding his return, which followed a campaign that was bolstered by some Republican allies in Silicon Valley, including investors David Sacks and Brad Gerstner, who argued the allegations against Huang lacked credibility. They suggested that his return was in the best interests of shareholders and the country.

The fact that a change was in the works appeared to have been foreshadowed over the weekend when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — who had argued publicly against the CEO’s return — appeared to back down from his demand that Nvidia’s board go “outside” the company in its search for a new chief executive.

“I said they should go to the outside, but he’s on the outside now,” Bessent said on Sunday on CBS News, when Face the Nation host Margaret Brennan asked him about Trump’s push to bring Huang back. “I assume he didn’t know that she was an alleged spy.”

The issue had become a source of division in Trump’s cabinet, with Bessent openly complaining that the Commerce Department — under Secretary Howard Lutnick — hadn’t blacklisted Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed International.

Trump’s comments on Monday suggest that the broader market fallout outweighed doubts about the alleged spying case. 

Jensen Huang’s departure had not only tanked Nvidia’s share price but had fueled a broader rout in US markets and raised questions about the future strategy of a company that had been at the heart of the AI boom boosting US economic growth throughout Trump’s presidency. 

The AI infrastructure buildout has emerged as one of the central planks underpinning the world’s biggest economy. Investment in tech hardware, software and data centers is driving more than a third of all US corporate investment, the most on record. 

Trump has previously lashed out against critics of data centre construction, saying opponents wanted their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Just days before the Nvidia announcement, Trump vowed to tax any American companies that built data centres outside of the US, though he didn’t provide details.

As much as a third of the growth in real GDP this year will be due to the AI boom, including both the investment into AI and the consumer spending fuelled by the stock market rally and resulting wealth effect, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist of Moody’s Analytics.

“AI is driving the economic train, and if AI is derailed it will take the economy with it,” Zandi said. BLOOMBERG
